Tests for {@link LoessInterpolator}, which implements the LOESS (Locally Weighted Scatterplot Smoothing) algorithm.

The tests cover:

  • Correctness on trivial inputs (single point, two points, straight line)
  • Smoothing quality on noisy sine data
  • Effect of bandwidth and robustness iterations on smoothness
  • Regression tests against reference output from R's {@code loess()}
  • Input validation (unequal sizes, empty data, non-monotonic x, non-finite values, out-of-range bandwidth)
Fraction of data points used in each local regression window.
Fraction of data points used for the Math-296 and MATH-1379 regression tests.
Number of robustness (re-weighting) iterations that down-weight outliers.
Convergence threshold for the iterative weight-update step.
A single data point must be returned unchanged: LOESS has no neighbours to regress against, so the smoothed value equals the observed value.
Two data points must each be returned unchanged: with only two points the local linear fit passes exactly through both.
LOESS must reproduce a perfectly straight line exactly (up to floating-point rounding), because any local linear fit of points on a line is that same line.
Smoothing noisy sine data should reduce the residual relative to the true sine more than the raw (noisy) observations do, i.e. the fit is closer to the ground truth than the jittered input.
Sum of squared residuals from the true sine for noisy input vs. smoothed output.

A wider bandwidth considers more neighbours in each local fit, which produces a smoother (lower total variation) curve. The test verifies that the total squared successive-difference (a proxy for roughness) decreases as bandwidth increases from 0.1 to 0.5 to 1.0.
sum of squared successive differences

When outliers are present, more robustness iterations reduce their influence via iterative re-weighting, yielding a smoother result. The test verifies that total variation (sum of absolute successive differences) decreases as the number of robustness iterations grows from 0 to 3.
Introduce two outliers to stress-test robustness iteration down-weighting.
indexed by number of robustness iterations
x and y arrays must have the same length.
Empty x/y arrays cannot be smoothed.
x values must be strictly increasing — decreasing sequence is rejected.
x values must be strictly increasing — duplicate (tied) values are rejected.
NaN in x array is not a finite real number and must be rejected.
Positive infinity in x array must be rejected.
Negative infinity in x array must be rejected.
NaN in y array is not a finite real number and must be rejected.
Positive infinity in y array must be rejected.
Negative infinity in y array must be rejected.
A bandwidth of 0.1 over 12 data points yields fewer than 2 neighbours, which is insufficient for a local linear regression.
Bandwidth must be in [0, 1]; a negative value must be rejected.
Bandwidth must be in [0, 1]; a value greater than 1 must be rejected.
Regression test from MATH-296: verifies smoothed values against reference output from R (rounded to three decimal places), using uniformly spaced x and no observation weights.
Reference output from R's loess(), rounded to .001.

Regression test from MATH-1379: verifies smoothed values against R reference output using unevenly spaced x values and no observation weights.

R command: {@code predict(loess(y ~ x, data.frame(x=xval, y=yval), span=0.35, degree=1, family="symmetric", control=loess.control(iterations=1, surface="direct")))}

Note: R counts all iterations, whereas {@code LoessInterpolator} robustness iterations are in addition to the initial fit, so {@code robustnessIters=0} in Java corresponds to {@code iterations=1} in R.
Reference output from R (see method Javadoc for the exact R command).

Regression test from MATH-1379: verifies smoothed values against R reference output using unevenly spaced x values and non-uniform observation weights.

R command: {@code predict(loess(y ~ x, data.frame(x=xval, y=yval), weights, span=0.35, degree=1, family="symmetric", control=loess.control(iterations=1, surface="direct")))}

Note: R counts all iterations, whereas {@code LoessInterpolator} robustness iterations are in addition to the initial fit, so {@code robustnessIters=0} in Java corresponds to {@code iterations=1} in R.
Weights < 1 in the middle and end of the range reduce those points' influence.
Reference output from R (see method Javadoc for the exact R command).

Populates {@code xval} and {@code yval} with noisy sine-wave data over one full period ({@code [0, 2π]}). The x spacing is jittered by {@code xnoise} and each y value is perturbed by uniform noise scaled by {@code ynoise}. @param xval output array for x coordinates (must be pre-allocated) @param yval output array for y values (must be pre-allocated, same length as xval) @param xnoise relative amplitude of random jitter added to x spacing @param ynoise absolute amplitude of additive uniform noise on y values
